status: Reviewed source-fit authoring resolution for A3.6/A3.7 using existing claims and attributed case/task protocols; no new heritage topic.
scope: G2 A3.6/A3.7 ordinary community/family heritage channels; source-required specific FNMI family practice explicit.
sourceInterpretation: Actual A3.6/A3.7 clauses reread. They require identifying some ways heritage is passed through community/family practices, not a general cultural-transmission theory or every illustrative event. A3.7 retains at least one particular First Nation, Métis or Inuit family celebration/practice.

cases.authority: Stories told by Kathy Morgan, written by Ashlyn Kerr Sutcliffe, published by Toronto & York Region Métis Council.
cases.authorityCheck: Métis Nation of Ontario council-contacts page directly links tyrmc.org: https://www.metisnation.org/community-councils/council-contacts/
cases.verifiedFacts: The account describes Kathy learning family/Métis history through conversations with her mother and grandmother. It also recounts family attendance at Métis events and learning from music, gatherings and shared experiences.
cases.childFacingSummary: Kathy describes hearing her family’s history from her mother and grandmother. The next person could learn it because family members shared and remembered the stories. A family member also describes learning about Métis culture at events attended with relatives.
cases.channel: Family conversations and shared community experiences carry knowledge to another generation.
cases.limits: One attributed family account, not every Métis family or a definition of Métis citizenship. The interviewer explicitly identifies as non-Indigenous; learning about a relative’s culture does not automatically confer that identity. Use the short age-appropriate paraphrase, not the unrelated adult material on the whole page.

cases.authority: Dylan Roy, Reference Archivist, official Library and Archives Canada blog (2024).
cases.verifiedFacts: The author follows a recipe from a 1909 cookbook assembled by St. Luke’s Woman’s Auxiliary in Sault Ste. Marie. The book remains available through the archive/library catalogue.
cases.childFacingSummary: People in a Sault Ste. Marie community collected recipes in a book long ago. In 2024, an archivist used that surviving book to learn how to prepare one of the dishes. Written records can help later people learn a practice even when the original writer is not there.
cases.channel: Community publication and preservation let another generation learn practical knowledge.
cases.limits: This is documented recipe sharing/recreation, not proof of an uninterrupted annual family custom or a practice of every ethnic group. The social-studies task does not require cooking, copying the recipe or reproducing source images.

cases.authority: Nipissing First Nation’s own culture/language resource.
cases.verifiedFacts: The Nation describes community classes with fluent speakers and language/cultural teaching in children’s programmes.
cases.childFacingSummary: Nipissing First Nation describes fluent speakers helping others learn Anishinaabemwin, and language/cultural learning in children’s programmes. A community can share its own knowledge by teaching and using it together.
cases.channel: Community teaching and shared use support cultural continuity.
cases.limits: A particular First Nation’s programme, not all communities or proof of a particular child’s attainment. Learn about the method; no target-language pronunciation/proficiency or paid resource access is required.

protocols.task: Use the attributed cases to identify what knowledge/practice is shared, who shares/learns it and how the community activity or surviving source lets later people learn. Compare oral conversations, written records and community teaching/gatherings; describe the actual channel rather than just name a holiday/food.
protocols.positive: Identifies multiple concrete ways cultural/community knowledge is passed through the provided practices, with correct source/people attribution.
protocols.nearMiss: Only names a food, language or event with no account of how people learn/share it, or generalizes one case to all peoples.
protocols.transfer: Another ordinary source-supported community practice with a different channel, identifying what is preserved/shared rather than copying a phrase.
protocols.scopeBoundary: The mandatory source asks identifying some ways. No abstract theory of culture, genetic-inheritance comparison, ceremony participation or universal narrative structure is imported.
protocols.sourceFit: Reviewed authoring coverage; tasks identify concrete attributed channels without requiring pupil-language competence or collecting learner records.

protocols.materials: Use the verified Métis family practice plus another ordinary family celebration/practice supplied as an attributed source/account or a voluntary non-sensitive family example. Identify family members/relationships without assuming one household form or asking for private testimony. A clearly labelled fictional ordinary practice may rehearse the operation, but the FNMI qualifier uses the verified actual case.
protocols.task: Describe the relevant family practice and identify who shares what with another generation and how the shared celebration/practice carries it. Compare the family conversation/gathering channel with another family practice, retaining the actual FNMI case rather than replacing it with a generic family story.
protocols.positive: Identifies several concrete family sharing/learning practices, including the specific Métis family account, without assuming cultural membership from ancestry or participation alone.
protocols.nearMiss: Only names relatives or a celebration; omits the sharing/learning channel or the required attributed FNMI family practice.
protocols.transfer: A different family practice/account while keeping its people, evidence and channel distinct.
protocols.scopeBoundary: No learner language/ceremony performance or compulsory own-family disclosure is required by this clause. The source’s actual identification requirement is separated from broader cultural-transmission theory.
protocols.sourceFit: Reviewed authoring coverage; tasks identify concrete attributed channels without requiring pupil-language competence or collecting learner records.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Explicitly explains how surviving objects, documents and stories allow later people to know past lives. Directly supports the oral/written channels in the family account and community cookbook.
wholeClaimReview.limit: Does not by itself establish every cultural practice or all contemporary language teaching.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Its own-family relationship/origin claim contributes a relationship component when interpreting Kathy’s family account; the account does not demonstrate the pupil’s own-family whole claim.
wholeClaimReview.limit: Do not infer whole own-family attainment or membership from understanding another family; naming relatives alone does not establish a sharing/learning channel.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Describes shared family/community celebrations and how they are marked. The resource task identifies which shared actions let people learn a practice.
wholeClaimReview.limit: A celebration label alone is not the required heritage-channel identification.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Continuity/change across family childhoods can support another comparative task.
wholeClaimReview.limit: No implicit universal cultural-transmission theory or all historic causes inferred.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Technology changes household work/travel/communication; relevant to a separately supported change case.
wholeClaimReview.limit: Technology is one possible cause, not a required explanation for every tradition.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Narrative structure/retelling is a separate operation, not proof of heritage knowledge.
wholeClaimReview.limit: Do not impose a fixed beginning/middle/end on all Métis oral traditions; use clear factual description of the sharing practice here.

wholeClaimReview.contribution: Clearly describe actual people, events and how the resource-supported practice is shared.
wholeClaimReview.limit: Generic eloquence does not replace the factual resource/heritage relationship.

CanadianRenewalBoundary: Approved mt_gSBJxNBQh3 remains the specific Canadian colonial-disruption→community-led renewal→identity claim, not generic transmission equivalence. Use it only for an actual relationship-supported case or a clearly labelled component; no authored expansion is proposed. Its planned G2 A1.4 reuse is a separate dependency.
curationRecommendation: Reuse approved after full mandatory-clause, existing-claim and primary-case review. The bounded identification tasks account for A3.6/A3.7 without a general transmission theory node. This is authoring coverage, not pupil attainment.
provenanceAndLimits: Primary-attributed sources read 2026-11-10; public factual paraphrases only. Cases demonstrate particular channels and do not represent every family/community. No source images, restricted curriculum wording, private records or direct pupil browsing requirements are included.
consumerBoundary: No canonical topic/association/learner-state changes in this dossier checkpoint; no language proficiency or community membership inferred.
